title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is one of training-data provenance: an AI music generation system was trained on recorded music without obtaining licenses from the rights holders. This is a deployment-stage issue that originates in how the model was built. The allegations center on Udio using copyrighted recordings, including specific named songs, to teach the system to produce similar-sounding compositions, then offering that capability to millions of users commercially.

The litigation involves multiple parties at different stages. Universal Music Group settled and entered a licensing arrangement. Warner Music Group also settled and announced a collaboration. Sony Music pursued a separate new lawsuit after a court declined to let it add over 30,000 recordings to its original case, and independent artists brought a class-action that a court declined to dismiss but transferred jurisdictions. A musicians' union also brought claims against UMG over its settlement with Udio.

What is not established is that any court has yet found Udio liable for copyright infringement, that the full scope of allegedly copied material has been adjudicated, or that any of the financial demands in the lawsuits represent final judgments. Settlements resolve disputes without constituting admissions, and allegations of copying 30,000 recordings remain allegations until a court rules on them.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, reaching licensing agreements to resolve disputes over copyrighted music used to train the company's AI model. The lawsuit claimed Udio improperly used songs like The Temptations' "My Girl" to create similar compositions without permission or payment. Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year trained exclusively on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to customize, stream, and share their creations while compensating artists.

The collaboration marks Udio's first major licensing deal with a record label and reflects growing tensions between the music industry and AI companies over copyright infringement. Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees and backed by investors including will.i.am and Andreessen Horowitz, has attracted millions of users since its launch. The financial terms remain undisclosed. Additionally, UMG announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers, signaling the industry's cautious embrace of AI technology when properly licensed.
